name: Secure Coding Common Pitfalls
description: This module lists frequently observed mistakes, bugs, and anti-patterns seen in everyday secure coding work, so they can be recognized and avoided during typical secure coding tasks.
content:
This module lists frequently observed mistakes, bugs, and anti-patterns seen in everyday secure coding work, so they can be recognized and avoided during typical secure coding tasks.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When secure coding decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
2. When secure coding guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
3. Prefer the simplest secure coding approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
4. Keep secure coding outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
5. Check that secure coding terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
6. Re-check edge cases relevant to secure coding (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
7. Before starting secure coding work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
8. When multiple secure coding strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
9. State assumptions about secure coding explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
10. Document any non-obvious secure coding decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
11. Surface known limitations of a chosen secure coding approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
12. Measure before optimizing any secure coding bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not silently drop secure coding edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid mixing unrelated secure coding concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not skip documenting secure coding assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not apply generic secure coding advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid introducing new secure coding abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
Revisit these secure coding guidelines if the task's constraints change significantly during the work.
